papers.title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
papers.abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920-0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875-0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672-0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

papers.title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
papers.abstract: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

papers.title: Autonomous generalizability auditing of scientific foundation models
papers.abstract: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models.

papers.title: brisc: a multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets have grown from tens of thousands of cells to tens of millions. At this scale, standard toolkits like Scanpy and Seurat need hours per analysis, hindering iterative exploration. We present brisc, the first end-to-end multithreaded CPU toolkit for single-cell analysis, spanning dimensionality reduction, integration, label transfer, clustering, embedding, differential expression and plotting. Unlike GPU-based counterparts, brisc strictly guarantees reproducibility: identical results between runs, regardless of thread count. Algorithmic innovations include a blocked inverted-file-index-based nearest-neighbors algorithm that makes 81-98% fewer errors than Scanpy and Seurat. On a 192-CPU node, brisc ran a standard workflow on 10 million cells in 3 minutes, 116x faster than Scanpy at under half its peak memory usage and 236x faster than Seurat with BPCells. On 96 CPUs, it matched the speed of rapids-singlecell on four H100 GPUs. brisc enables near-real-time, reproducible analysis of tens of millions of cells without specialized hardware.

papers.title: HiFiTaxa: a reproducible analysis pipeline for full length 16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing from PacBio reads
papers.abstract: Long-read amplicon sequencing profiles communities at high resolution, but taxonomic accuracy depends on the reference, classifier and the parameters used. Here, we present HiFiTaxa, a reproducible, single command Nextflow pipeline for PacBio HiFi 16S rRNA gene and fungal ITS amplicons. It builds versioned references from current GTDB and UNITE releases and supports Bayesian lowest common ancestor (BLCA) and naive Bayes (NB) classifiers and the read level profilers Emu (16S rRNA gene) and EMITS (ITS). We benchmarked them on mock communities and on holdouts with 10% of GTDB or UNITE databases sequences withheld. On the 16S rRNA gene mock of 20 species, BLCA detected all 20 species and reported two false positives, NB detected 17 and reported none, and Emu detected all 20 and reported eight. In the GTDB holdout, for taxa represented in the reference, BLCA reached 80.0% species level accuracy against 48.1% for the exact matching species step of NB. However, NB produced fewer incorrect assignments for taxa absent from the reference. On fungal ITS, BLCA had slightly higher holdout accuracy at species level(54.7%) against 52.2% for NB. NB was more conservative for novel taxa, and EMITS detected the most mock species. HiFiTaxa therefore offers a single reproducible workflow that uses current GTDB and UNITE releases and enables users to choose between different classifier algorithms depending on their needs.

papers.title: Error-Controlled Discovery of Protein Interactions via Conformal Calibration
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

papers.title: Representation-aware calibration enables statistically reliable protein structure search
papers.abstract: Searching large databases of predicted protein structures can reveal remote homologs, but reliable discovery requires accurate significance estimates. We show that native E-values reported by protein structure search tools such as Foldseek and Reseek can be unreliable, leading to false discoveries or missed homologs. To address this problem, we introduce Struct-Caliper, which provides reliable query-specific p-values for protein structure search. The method uses representation-aware query randomization to generate background queries and compares observed alignment scores with the highest scores from randomized searches of the same database. In simulations, SG p-values generally kept reported false positive at or below the chosen cutoff under the evaluated randomization procedures. In searches of 15,177 ASTRAL40 structures, SG p-values increased Foldseek homolog recovery by 18.2% with slightly fewer false discoveries compared with native E-values at a cutoff of 0.01. For Reseek, false discoveries even decreased by 99.5%. Across 73 queries searched against more than two million AlphaFoldDB structures, SG p-values increased the mean recovery of DALI-supported matches by 23.5% at the same cutoff. These results show that Struct-Caliper can improve the reliability of structure searches and help prioritize discoveries for further biological analysis.

papers.title: Evaluating the Identifiability of Temporal Delay and Response Attenuation in Endometrial Decidualization
papers.abstract: Endometriosis is associated with impaired endometrial decidualization, yet conventional differential expres-sion analyses cannot readily distinguish delayed transcriptional activation from reduced response amplitude.These mechanisms may produce similar expression differences at individual time points while implying distinct biological interpretations. Establishing when they can be distinguished is therefore a computational identifiability problem.We implement an identifiability-aware analysis of temporal displacement and amplitude attenuation in longitudinal transcriptomic responses. The approach combines reference trajectories, constrained amplitude-only and amplitude-plus-delay models, analytical examples of observational equivalence, and simulation-based assessments of mechanism distinguishability. Held-out time-point evaluation and culture-level sensitivity analyses examine the stability of model-dependent conclusions.In GSE246591, a candidate-delay-dependent dynamic-range filter excluded 30.9 - 38.3% of initially dynamic features under a hypothetical 24-hour shift across four endometrial stromal cultures. A two-component diagnostic separating retained dynamic range from affine shape similarity revealed that small projection residuals can arise from either loss of observable dynamics or similarity of response shapes. These findings demonstrate why a single separation statistic may be insufficient for interpreting temporal identifiability.Complementary independent in vivo analyses provided biological context. In GSE51981, an endometrial progesterone-response-associated transcriptional score was reduced in endometriosis samples (phase-model estimate 0.155, 95% CI 0.222 to 0.088). GSE6364 showed a directionally consistent but statistically inconclusive difference (0.033, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.002). Neither observation independently establishes a temporal delay.Together, these results support selection-aware evaluation of temporal transcriptomic responses, distin-guishing structural ambiguity and loss of dynamic signal from evidence of a biological timing change.

papers.title: Missing by design: why genomic metadata must be captured at submission, not recovered from the literature
papers.abstract: Plant and metazoan genome assemblies are being deposited in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC) archives at an accelerating rate, but the biological context needed to interpret them, such as ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure, is often missing from the record: these attributes are optional in most submission checklists and, when supplied, are entered as free text. We describe the gap in three layers. Ploidy varies within a species and cannot be inferred from taxonomy; chromosome-naming conventions differ between assemblies of the same crop; and that inconsistency is concentrated in species named by subgenome and is not associated with the size of the research community, which points to the lack of a shared convention. As a case study, we built a pipeline that recovers these attributes from the publications linked to an assembly. On a benchmark of 82 assemblies, its current version reported one wrong ploidy, and across 1,059 plant assemblies an earlier, less strict version found the ploidy in a publication for about half; for nearly a third, it found a publication but no statement of ploidy in it. Recovery from the literature can annotate assemblies already deposited but cannot stop new ones from arriving incomplete. We therefore propose that ploidy, cultivar, and subgenome structure be captured at submission as mandatory, controlled-vocabulary attributes, building on existing INSDC and Genomic Standards Consortium checklists.

papers.title: gcat, its_a_scam: modular tools for single cell data processing and per-cellquality control
papers.abstract: Motivation: The era of designing bioinformatic pipelines using open source tools is giving way to monolithic, and often proprietary, tools designed for end-to-end analysis, especially in the context of single cell data. While these tools are convenient for going from sequencing data to an almost complete data analysis "in a few clicks", they can strongly limit data use beyond standard analyses Results: We developed Gene and Chromosome Analysis Toolkit (gcat) and It's a scam To Sell Another Single Cell Analysis Method (its_a_scam) for modular processing and quality control of single cell genomic data, freeing users from their reliance on proprietary tools. gcat is a C++ library for parsing genomic data and working with it over genomic coordinates. its_a_scam is built on top of gcat and provides a suite of tools for a wide range of single cell data processing and quality control. its_a_scam can be used in conjunction with commonly used open source tools for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq count matrix generation, and for performing per-cell quality control directly from alignment files. These alignment-level per-cell metrics can be used for quality control of each cell or to understand celltype differences post-clustering or post-annotation. Using a peripheral blood mononuclear cell Multiome dataset, we show that the count matrices generated with the aid of its_a_scam are highly concordant with those generated by proprietary pipelines. The alignment metrics further demonstrate celltype differences in aligned genomic regions, metagene profiles, and genebody coverage. The modular nature of its_a_scam allows users to integrate it into their existing pipelines, while also enabling analysis beyond current pipelines. Availability: gcat (distributed as gcatlib) and its_a_scam are open source and available at https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/gcatlib and https://github.com/rishvanth-kp/its_a_scam. Detailed documentation is available at https://gcatlib.readthedocs.io/ and https://its-a-scam.readthedocs.io.

papers.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences it generates rather than treating the model as a black box. Candidate sequences were filtered based on predicted Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) along with human insights into the structural activities of the AMPs in bacterial membranes, and a final set of peptides was selected for experimental testing. Biological assays for determining MIC confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, with fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements providing structural insight. With our XSI approach, we are able to reveal correlations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties of these sequences to bacterial membrane mimics, that directly correlate with biological activities in cell-based assays. This builds confidence in that the learned amino acid interdependencies as applied to AMPs carries physico-chemical meaning and is relevant for discoveries of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can serve as effective and transparent tools for rational AMP discovery.

papers.title: Single-cell geometry of drug responses across malignant glioma states
papers.abstract: Malignant gliomas exhibit substantial transcriptional heterogeneity: AC-, OPC-, NPC- and MES-like states can coexist within the same tumor, and a drug affecting one state may leave others relatively unaffected. Whether these states respond in a shared direction, or diverge, is rarely tested directly, since drug response is usually summarized by one score that collapses this heterogeneity. A public single-cell RNA-sequencing resource of drug-treated glioma slice cultures (391,444 cells) is reanalyzed here to test this directly. After restricting to 252,106 transformed glioma cells, 43 treatment-vehicle comparisons from 19 TissueID-defined units are evaluated for response-direction coherence (C, similarity of state-conditioned treatment vectors) and change in state separation (K, state-centroid contraction or expansion). C proves to be the reproducible signal: it survives high-confidence state filtering (r=0.931), an independently selected 500-gene space (r=0.634), the published Neftel modules (r=0.783) and non-overlapping gene cross-fitting (r=0.809), and exceeds two null models in 41 of 43 comparisons, a result that also holds across the 19 biological units themselves (19 of 19 positive; P=3.8e-6). Within-drug coherence exceeds between-drug coherence in all 52 drug pairs and all 11 multi-drug units (P=0.000488): response direction is drug-specific, not generic. K tells a different story: stable only when the feature space is fixed, it loses concordance whenever that space shifts, with only about half of comparisons separating from the null. Malignant glioma states largely agree on the direction of drug response even when they disagree on its magnitude.

papers.title: All-Atom Structure Tokenizer: AtomLM-9b for Biomolecular Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction.

papers.title: Rho: A Purpose-Driven Workspace for Human-AI Collaborative Analysis
papers.abstract: Agent-assisted bioinformatics has moved the bottleneck from computing a result to judging it: whether a comparison answers the intended question, on which unit of replication, at which version of the input, and what would change the conclusion. These judgments need materials that are usually scattered across conversations, notebooks, figures, run logs and notes, while the agent's context is a transcript rather than the structure the researcher is actually reading. We present Rho, a human--AI collaborative analysis environment that organizes materials by the current scientific purpose: it selects or obtains the materials a judgment needs, declares the relations they serve, composes operable views, and makes this organization a shared state that is at once the researcher's reading interface and the agent's continuation context. We present the design in three parts: a method object---the operations that form a round-trip, the kinds of state that must stay distinct, and the protocol invariants that make each distinction checkable; a three-layer architecture that separates capability providers from the application that composes them; and five illustrative analyses on public data. In a bulk RNA-seq case the recomputed counts differed from the published counts and the interface kept the computation, the choices and the discrepancy available for inspection; a single-nucleus case makes sample-level replication visible behind a cell-level comparison. Under one configuration these analyses show how the design behaves in practice; we present the work as a design contribution rather than an evaluation, and usability, comparative benefit and the scientific validity of individual analyses remain to be evaluated.

papers.title: Peptorama: Structure creation and exploratory data analysis for non-ribosomal peptides
papers.abstract: Non-ribosomal peptides (NRPs) are a diverse family of compounds with many clinical and biotechnological uses. NRP biodiscovery increasingly focuses on biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), and NRP structures can generally be predicted from BGCs. Despite their chemical connection, there is no individual research tool which quickly analyses NRPs and BGCs in combination. Here, we present Peptorama, which simplifies drawing diverse NRP structures and allows rapid comparisons between known and predicted NRPs. We show the utility of peptide comparisons and interactive analysis for biodiscovery, exemplified by retrospective analysis of calcium dependent antibiotics and biodiscovery of novel pyoverdine producing candidate strains. Peptide comparisons are computationally more efficient than BGC comparisons, substantially cutting runtimes without loss of biodiscovery functionality. Peptorama can therefore enhance existing pipelines with a rapid method for comparing peptide-level diversity. It is available online at https://peptorama.com/ and is also available to be run locally.

papers.title: Comparative Transcriptomic Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Neutrophils from Rheumatoid Arthritis and COVID-19
papers.abstract: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective: To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods: Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results: In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions: RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.

papers.title: Deterministic DNA-first discovery reveals recurrent genomic architectures
papers.abstract: Genome mining typically begins with known genes or protein families, which can make systems defined primarily by genomic organization difficult to detect. We developed a DNA-first framework combining asymmetric-covariance natural-vector representations with generic positional recurrence, joining separately calibrated signals through genomic coordinates. In benchmarks of array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) loci, the target-free mathematical arm localized seven of eight predeclared loci, including all seven with exact-array coordinates. Dual-arm signals occurred in none of three non-array RT controls and in one of five UG27 systems, indicating selectivity within these small control sets. A separate profile-guided search of 6.12 Gb identified five candidate array-associated RT-like systems. In an independent 54.38-Gb evaluation of this profile-guided arm, structural compatibility was 24/32 under a historical-rule mirror, 12/32 after novelty-only selection, and 0/17 for architecture-selected complete ORFs; the two 32-member panels shared six exact sequences. Together, these results suggest that mathematical features of raw DNA can complement protein-directed searches in nominating genomic architectures for experimental RNA-to-DNA studies.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: Optimiser Repairs for Living-Cell Self-Driving Laboratories: Performance and Redundancy under Experimental Constraints
papers.abstract: Living-cell self-driving laboratories must optimise experiments despite delayed readouts, changing responses and limited sample availability. In simulations, we evaluate when optimiser repairs improve closed-loop performance and when platform constraints make them redundant, separating consumption of a sample from permanent loss of the ability to repeat its condition. We prove that exclusions and confirmation requests produce exactly the baseline trajectory when they act only on conditions already forbidden by the platform, share the same posterior and selection procedure, and release infeasible requested slots. This result covers the evaluated pending-exclusion, previous-batch and confirmation rules under permanent condition retirement; it does not cover arbitrary selection interventions. We then conduct 33,900 simulated policy runs with 200-300 paired campaign seeds per setting. A public PBMC reference supports characterisation of the target-label readout, while condition-response landscapes remain synthetic. Across 27 landscape, assay-size and kernel settings, previous-batch exclusion changes final normalised performance by -0.004 to +0.283, with positive differences surviving Holm adjustment in 13 settings. Effects are small on the rugged landscape. Permanent retirement can be harmful under noisy rugged responses. All three subsumed interventions reproduce every saved baseline event on 200 of 200 paired seeds. These results establish the importance of explicit availability constraints and evaluation across experimental regimes when assessing optimiser repairs.

papers.title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

papers.title: CloneVI: A deep generative model for deciphering the relationships between cell state and mitochondrial genotype
papers.abstract: Cellular diversity arises from both genetic lineages and non-genetic regulation of cell states, and knowing which cell states are tied to lineages is central to understanding how clones shape disease. Single-cell multi-omics technologies measure mitochondrial DNA mutations together with gene expression or chromatin accessibility in the same cells, but clones are usually inferred from mutations alone, making such clones difficult to identify. We developed CloneVI, a deep generative model that infers clonal structure from a latent cell state derived from gene expression or chromatin accessibility. It estimates the clonal probability of each cell from this cell state, together with the allele frequency of each clone by reconstructing the observed mutation counts. In simulated data, CloneVI recovered the ground-truth clonal structure in both single-clone and mixed-clone cell populations. In clonal hematopoiesis single-cell RNA-seq data with enriched mitochondrial transcripts, the inferred clones were associated with specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, and some of them showed high expression of a T-cell receptor variable-region gene. In chronic lymphocytic leukemia mitochondrial single-cell ATAC-seq data, CloneVI separated populations with different heteroplasmy levels and identified increased PAX9 accessibility. In a multi-donor ovarian tumor cohort, CloneVI captured mutant-cell populations enriched in particular cell states, and a differential test weighted by the clonal probability revealed the transcription factor activity of the cell state in which the mutant cells concentrated. CloneVI thus identifies populations defined by mitochondrial DNA mutations and associated with cell states in single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data. CloneVI is available at https://github.com/TaichiHIBI/cloneVI.

papers.title: NORMA 3.0: aesthetic and group-aware visualization and analysis of annotated biological networks
papers.abstract: Summary: Interpreting a biological network often rests on the relationship between its connectivity and the functional groups annotated on it, such as pathways, complexes, or enriched terms. For example, whether a group forms a cohesive module, how groups overlap, and which proteins connect them. These relationships are often hard to assess visually when groups are numerous or overlap, and most tools represent membership only by node color. NORMA 3.0 is a complete client-side rewrite of its predecessors, delineating and laying out groups with convex hulls, bubble sets, or fog clouds. Multi-group nodes are rendered as pies and directed, and parallel edges retain their evidence channels. Eighteen 2D and nine 3D layouts are scored by silhouette width, outline intrusion and overlap, and benchmarked for group separation and run time. The implementation also includes edge bundling, network importers for six databases, 21 topological measures, group-level and enrichment statistics, comparison of up to ten networks, export of high-resolution images, and an Application Programming Interface. Availability and implementation: NORMA 3.0 is freely available at https://normaviz.org. The source code is available at https://github.com/PavlopoulosLab/NORMA.

papers.title: Long read sequencing reveals changes in measured isoform structure and abundance due to RNA processing
papers.abstract: Oxford Nanopore Technology enables direct RNA sequencing without reverse transcription (RT) and cDNA sequencing without PCR amplification, allowing investigation of how RNA preparation protocols bias sequencing data. PCR amplification is known to introduce biases related to expression levels, transcript lengths, and GC content. However, biases introduced by RT have been described more recently and their quantification remains more elusive. Using seven cell line datasets from SG-NEx, we compared nanopore sequencing of direct RNA, direct cDNA, and PCR-amplified cDNA. We identified hundreds of differentially expressed genes and isoforms between protocols, indicating significant changes in observed expression. Differentially expressed isoforms displayed expected amplification biases, and further we observed decreased PCR counts associated with higher m6A methylation levels on native RNA. We also found differential transcript usage in hundreds of genes across cell lines, showing substantial changes in measured isoform proportions between protocols. Analysis of structural differences between isoforms that switch dominance revealed that while some events involve simple RNA fragmentation, most involve complex structural differences including novel junctions (e.g. exon skipping, intron retention). Compared to non-DTU genes, inserted introns (exitrons) were significantly more common after RT and amplification. Furthermore, visualisation of raw coverage data proved crucial for qualitative validation of experimental findings.

papers.title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
papers.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. Existing segmentation methods focus on delineating cell boundaries, yet transcripts that diffuse beyond their cell of origin, fall where cells overlap, or lie in bins that cells only partially cover are still misassigned. Here we present Tracel, a two-stage optimal transport framework that assigns spatial observations to cells under the guidance of a matched single-cell RNA-sequencing reference. Tracel first aligns reference cells to spatial cells to estimate the expected expression profile at each cell location, and then maps transcripts to cells against these profiles. The same formulation assigns transcripts from imaging-based platforms (e.g., Xenium, CosMx) and bin counts from sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Visium HD). Across five human datasets spanning three platforms and three tissues, Tracel improves the separation of cell types over existing methods, assigning cell-type markers to their correct cells, retaining more cell-intrinsic transcripts and reducing contamination from neighboring cells. Tracel also preserves variation within cell types, yielding more accurate differential expression across spatial locations, and its expression profiles attribute ligand-receptor interactions to the correct cell-type pairs in cell-cell communication analysis. Tracel can enter the segmentation workflow at different stages, either refining an existing segmentation or segmenting cells starting from nucleus segmentation.

papers.title: Disentangling Context-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Progression Signatures through an Explainable AI Framework
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression involves stage-dependent transcriptional changes that are often masked by dominant cellular and biological variation. Here, we present ADVISE (Alzheimer's Disease Variational Isolation of Signal Embeddings), an interpretable deep generative framework designed to disentangle Braak stage-associated transcriptional signals from background biological variation through separate latent representations. Using explainable AI, ADVISE prioritizes genes and pathways contributing to the disease-specific representation. Applying ADVISE to large-scale single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from the human prefrontal cortex, we identify shared and context-specific signatures of AD progression across global, sex-specific, and cell-type-specific analyses, revealing convergent molecular programs involving synaptic transmission, HSF1-associated proteostatic stress responses, and SLIT/ROBO axon guidance. Notably, ADVISE prioritizes ROBO2 as a progression-associated candidate in excitatory neurons. Experimental validation using CRISPR activation in hiPSC-derived excitatory neurons demonstrates that ROBO2 activation reduces the phosphorylated Tau-to-total Tau ratio. ADVISE thus reveals context-dependent molecular signatures of AD progression and bridges human single-cell discoveries with experimental validation of candidate regulators of AD pathology.

papers.title: Uncovering cross-signal interactions in single-cell and spatial omics
papers.abstract: Individual cells simultaneously encode multiple biological signals in their gene expression profiles, including spatial position, circadian phase, and disease state. These signals can be entangled in complex ways, including circadian patterns that vary along disease progression and cell cycle dynamics that shift along developmental trajectories. While methods to disentangle such signals have been recently developed, characterizing the interaction itself between multicellular signals along with its effects on tissue function, localizing cellular subpopulations which exhibit signal interactions, and identifying potential candidate genes which drive such interactions, all remain major challenges. We present CRISP which characterizes signal interactions in single-cell gene expression data based on the correspondence between the multiple, probabilistic signal-specific projections of the data. Across simulations with tunable couplings and four single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets, CRISP recovers diverse biological signal interactions and localizes them to informative cellular subpopulations and groups of associated genes; CRISP distinguishes healthy from fibrotic liver samples and localizes the loss of zonation-position coupling to individual fibrotic hepatocytes, resolves the asymmetric coupling of TGF-{beta} response, EMT, and cell-cycle phase to specific cell subpopulations, and flags transcriptionally delayed hepatocytes in Plasmodium liver infection. Beyond quantifying and localizing signal interactions, CRISP can refine existing labels, uncover continuous cellular transitions and reveal condition-associated genes.

papers.title: TensorPLS: an R package for exploring molecular and temporal patterns in longitudinal omics data using PLS-DA
papers.abstract: Longitudinal omics datasets combine high-dimensional repeated measurements with missing observations, complicating supervised modelling and temporal interpretation. We present TensorPLS, an R package integrating missing-data handling, matrix-based partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), structured variable importance, subject-level nested cross-validation and downstream functional enrichment. Data are represented as subjects x features x time tensors. Missing values are handled by Tucker3 reconstruction or feature-time mean imputation, after which tensors are unfolded along the subject mode for PLS-DA. Cumulative variable importance in projection (VIP) scores are mapped to feature-time coordinates and summarised across time and cumulative PLS models. During nested cross-validation, imputation, component tuning, VIP-based feature selection and refitting are performed within training partitions. Full-cohort models are fitted separately for descriptive interpretation. We evaluated TensorPLS on two public longitudinal transcriptomic datasets using five-by-five nested cross-validation. In GSE68310 (109 subjects), Tucker3 reconstruction yielded Q2Y = 0.670, AUROC 0.971 and balanced accuracy 0.931. In GSE182616 (66 subjects), feature-time mean imputation yielded Q2Y = 0.294, AUROC 0.827 and balanced accuracy 0.756. Predictive metrics were calculated from pooled outer held-out predictions. TensorPLS supports predictive assessment, functional enrichment of selected genes and temporal interpretation of model-assigned feature importance.

papers.title: PLATE: a global atlas of food metaplasmidomes
papers.abstract: Plasmids play a central role in the acquisition and spread of genes underlying important traits in food-associated microorganisms. Although shotgun metagenomics has greatly expanded opportunities to study food microbiomes, their plasmid diversity remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we present the Plasmid Atlas of Food Ecosystems (PLATE), a curated global resource of food metaplasmidomes. Built from 4,690 food metagenomes spanning 55 countries and 17 categories, PLATE comprises a broad catalog (bPLATE) of 3,904,895 putative plasmid contigs (PPCs) and a refined catalog (rPLATE) of 213,474 PPCs, corresponding to 181,871 unique sequences. Both catalogs are complemented by curated sample metadata, host predictions, taxonomic assignments, and functional annotations covering antimicrobial resistance (AMR), protein families and KEGG orthologs, CRISPR-Cas systems, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and bioactive peptides. We demonstrate PLATE's utility through a case study of AMR genes detected on PPCs from food microbiomes. PLATE is freely accessible and enables users to interactively search for and download sequences, annotations, and associated metadata. By organizing plasmid-associated sequence diversity and functional potential across food ecosystems, PLATE provides a foundation for analyses of food metaplasmidomes.

papers.title: SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming): a simulation-informed Nextflow pipeline for cross-study harmonisation of 16S rRNA metabarcoding datasets
papers.abstract: Global syntheses of 16S rRNA metabarcoding data rely on combining datasets, yet amplicon sequence variants generated with different primer pairs can rarely be compared directly. Existing approaches correct batch effects statistically or aggregate taxonomically; none first establishes whether the sequences are positionally comparable. We present SeCAT (Sequence Consensus Amplicon Trimming), a Nextflow pipeline that maps every studys variants onto a 16S rRNA full-length reference alignment, determines the largest window shared across studies, and tests by simulation whether trimming to that window degrades community structure before any data are merged. Applied to thirteen marine studies sequenced with three primer sets, twelve converged on a consensus window with a median trimmed read length of 249 bp (9,582 alignment columns). Degradation tests across twelve studies and six taxonomic ranks (72 study-rank combinations) returned 31 passes, 38 cautions and three confirmed failures. Eleven studies (682 samples after filtering) were harmonised (trimmed to the window and merged), collapsing 20,891 primer-specific variants into 12,667 MetaASVs, trimmed sequences deduplicated across studies. Harmonisation preserved community structure at family level (Mantel r = 1.00; Procrustes m{superscript 2} < 0.001) without adding between-study variance (|{Delta}R{superscript 2}| < 0.001). Alpha diversity, including observed richness, was recovered across all levels (intraclass correlations 0.93-1.00), whereas sequence-level congruence was moderate (Procrustes m{superscript 2} = 0.52), as expected where between-study similarity at sequence level exists only after harmonisation. The harmonised output supports synthesis from aggregated ranks down to exact sequences. By establishing positional comparability before merging, SeCAT opens the archive of primer-fragmented 16S rRNA surveys to sequence-level synthesis.
